newsitem.title: FRANCE: BA seeks court order on Paris airport security.
newsitem.headline: BA seeks court order on Paris airport security.

text.p: British Airways went to court in France on Monday to push for greater security at Charles de Gaulle airport after the state airline of strife-torn Algeria resumed flights to Paris.
British Airways closed its counters at the weekend after Air Algerie opened counters alongside it. The British airline has carried out check-in operations on the terminal roof and in a nearby hotel.
But passengers cannot check in their luggage, which must either be carried into the cabin or sent separately to its destination.

British Airways asked an administrative court in Versailles to order authorities to tighten security at Charles de Gaulle. British Airways and the Paris airports authority said a ruling was due on Tuesday.
British Airways wants Air Algerie counters moved away from its own operations, but airport authorities say security is already extra-tight and meets international standards.
The British carrier flies about 60 flights a day in and out of Paris.

Air Algerie resumed flights on Friday. It stopped flying to Paris two years ago in protest at being forced to use a remote terminal after Moslem radicals seized an Air France plane on the ground in Algiers and forced it to fly to France.
The four hijackers killed three passengers and were themselves shot dead by police commandos who stormed the plane in Marseille.
British Airways alleges the security arrangements for Air Algerie at Charles de Gaulle fall short of those at Marseille and other French airports where the airline has operated since.
A Paris airport spokeswoman told Reuters "if our security arrangements are suitable for (the Israeli airline) El Al, they should certainly be acceptable for BA."

Neither the airline nor the airport would go into details of security measures currently used. Troops already patrol the airport after a wave of bombings in France by Algerian Moslem extremists in 1995.
About 60,000 people have died in Algeria in widespread violence sparked by the cancellation of January 1992 elections which Moslem fundamentalists were set to win.

Several Algerian passengers flying on their national airline and interviewed on French television at Charles de Gaulle said leaders of the Algerian Islamic revolt were based in London and Britain should curb their activities there.
